answers.justification: Vans come from a shared pool (C6). The 19 complaining drivers logged 604 days, 141 of them on Upper Wend, in non-Northfield vans with no brake reports (C6, C7). Their training completion matches that of non-complainers (C12), and the LK-209 dashcam shows it was driven within limits (C15).

The Calder Road and in-house vans got the same Tessaro batches (T-0612/T-0703) and ran Upper Wend just as often, with zero soft-pedal reports (C3, C6, C14, E2). LK-217 and LK-224 stopped complaining after only their fluid was renewed and the pads were left alone (C9).

All 11 complaint vans are exactly the Northfield vans filled from the bay-3 bulk drum, which was open since March and had a missing cap (E2, C6, C9). The two warranty-return vans measured boiling points of 152°C and 149°C against 255°C for sealed stock, and their reports stopped after the fluid was renewed (C9, E2, C6).

The descents are a necessary trigger (C5, C15), but the 'otherwise sound brakes' part is contradicted. Vans with sound fluid ran the same descents without complaints, and the affected vans had water-contaminated fluid (C6, C9). Weather was cooling over the period (C10).

FleetCheck went live at all depots on 1 Aug (C8), yet soft-pedal reports cluster on specific Northfield vans (E2, C6). They are backed by measured fluid degradation (C9) and a near-miss on dashcam (C15), with zero reports at Eastgate in August under the app (E2).

The evidence covers every element: fluid fitted before symptoms appeared (C6, E2), a documented mechanism (C9), exact covariation with the bulk-drum vans (C6, C9), rivals ruled out by same-pad/same-route/same-driver comparisons (C3, C6, C14), and an intervention in which renewing the fluid on LK-217/224 ended their complaints (C9, C6, E2).
Seventeen Tessaro-fitted non-Northfield Eastgate vans (C3, C14) had no soft-pedal reports despite 9–16 Upper Wend days each (C6), and the pads were left untouched in the fix that worked (C9).

Noise reports rose and most were on Tessaro vans (E5, C13). However, Tessaro vans are by definition the freshly padded ones with no fresh-pad baseline for the old brand, and FleetCheck raised reporting across all categories (E5, C8).

The same drivers on the same routes had no problems in non-Northfield vans (C6, C7), training does not separate complainers from non-complainers (C12), and the LK-209 driving was within limits (C15). The harsh-braking rise in C1 cannot be attributed to individual vans or drivers.

This directly addresses the established cause, a safety hazard that has already produced a near-miss (C9, C15). The garage itself recommended rechecking these vans (C9), and the action is proportionate and reversible.

The drivers' reports correctly flagged real faulty vans (C6, C9). Disciplining them would punish the wrong party and suppress safety reporting, which drivers already say they are afraid to do (E4, C7).
The link between the pads and noise is only an association, confounded by fresh fitting and the FleetCheck rollout (E5, C8). The pads are not implicated in the soft-pedal problem (C3, C14).

This is a low-cost confirmatory check, since Eastgate has no tester (C4, C14). However, the non-Northfield vans used sealed fluid and have had no complaints (C3, C14, C6), so it is reasonable but not urgent.
The Northfield bulk-drum match, the boiling-point readings and the outcome of the fluid-renewal intervention (C6, C9, E2) together justify committing to A1 now.

ambiguousItems: Q4: Upper Wend descents are a necessary trigger (the vans are fine on the flat), so some reviewers may answer 'unknown' instead of 'contradicted'. It hinges on the 'otherwise in sound condition' clause.
Q13: A4 could be 'preferred' as a cheap safety check given that no boiling-point tester exists at Eastgate, or 'acceptable' since the non-Northfield vans used sealed fluid and have no complaints.
Q12: A3 could be read as 'acceptable', since the switch is low-harm, or 'premature', because the noise link is unproven.
caseProblems: The pattern is very clean: the 11 complaint vans are exactly the 11 Northfield bulk-drum vans, and both warranty vans stopped reporting just before the fix date. This is plausible but arguably too tidy.
LK-209's fluid was never tested ('vehicle inspection pending', C15). The near-miss vehicle itself is not confirmed, which slightly weakens certainty for that van.
The C6 remark 'see garage paperwork' points to C9, which holds the key evidence. The title is neutral, so no leak, but the case depends heavily on C9 and C6 together.

rulings.explanation: H4 makes two claims: the descents overheat the brakes, and those brakes are 'otherwise in sound condition'. The evidence goes directly against both. C6 shows all 38 Eastgate vans ran Upper Wend on 9–16 days each from a common pool, yet the 27 non-Northfield vans had no complaints. So the descents do not cause failure in sound brakes. C9 shows the complaint vans were not sound: their fluid boiled at 149–152°C against 255°C for sealed stock. Complaints also stopped after a fluid-only renewal while the vans kept running Upper Wend. That the descents expose the defect does not save H4, because H4 says the brakes are sound, and they are not. 'Unknown' means the evidence does not discriminate, and here it clearly does. 'Contradicted' is the only defensible answer.
rulings.fix: No change needed. Optional hardening: in the authoring notes, state explicitly that the descents trigger the symptoms but are not a sufficient cause in sound brakes, so 'contradicted' applies to the whole H4 claim.

rulings.explanation: A4 adds a boiling-point check at the next routine service for the non-Northfield vans. The evidence gives no sign that these vans have bad fluid. C6 accounts for all 38 vans: 13 Northfield, 12 Calder Road and 13 in-house. All the non-Northfield vans had fresh fluid from sealed 1 L bottles (C3, C14). They had no complaints despite matched Upper Wend exposure and the same drivers (C6). A4 is therefore a cheap, sensible precaution, but it does not address a known hazard, so it is not among the best next actions. A1 is clearly the best. 'Premature' does not fit, because A4 does not depend on committing to an unconfirmed hypothesis; it is a low-cost check. 'Harmful' also does not apply. 'Acceptable' is the only defensible answer.

The case for A3 rests entirely on R3 (Tessaro pads cause squeal). E5 itself shows that R3 is an association confounded by fresh-pad bedding-in and the FleetCheck reporting change. C13 (squeal mostly within three weeks of fitting) and C8 (noise reports up 64% alongside rises in every other category) point further toward confounding. A3 also costs about £21,400 a year (C11) and commits to a supplier change on an unestablished link. This matches the definition of 'premature' exactly: it could be right if the still-unconfirmed R3 were confirmed, but committing now is not justified. 'Acceptable' would require the action to be reasonable on the current evidence. Because the evidence does not establish that switching would reduce squeal, low harm alone does not make it reasonable. 'Premature' is the only defensible answer.
rulings.fix: No change needed. Optional hardening: add a clause to E5 saying the switch back would give up the procurement saving. That makes the cost of committing on an unproven link explicit.
